8:
SAY:
- "Today we need a pencil, a mini whiteboard with a texta, and our booklet."
- "Put them on your desk."

DO:
- Hold up each item.
- Wait until each student has them ready.

TEACHER NOTES:
Quick setup. Keep under 30 seconds.

WATCH FOR:
- Students still searching when teaching starts. Pause and reset.
9:
TEACHER NOTES:
Section divider for the shared read aloud. Move on quickly.
10:
SAY:
- "Today's text is called New Year's Celebrations Around the World."
- "This is information writing, not a story."
- "Ask: which countries do you think might be in this text? Expected: any guess."
- "Listen carefully. We will talk about it after."

DO:
- Display the title.
- Take 2 to 3 student predictions.
- Promise students they will see lots of different countries.

TEACHER NOTES:
The big question is 'why do people in different countries have such different ways of celebrating the new year?' Anticipated answers: different cultures, beliefs, climates, history, family traditions. Activate prior knowledge by asking how families celebrate the new year.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who name countries they know. Affirm and listen for which ones come up in the text.
11:
SAY:
- "In Spain, families gather at midnight with a bowl of grapes."
- "As the clock chimes twelve times, they quickly eat twelve grapes, one for each month."
- "Finishing them all in time is said to bring good luck."
- "Ask: what do families in Spain eat at midnight? Expected: twelve grapes."

DO:
- Read the page aloud.
- Pause after 'the year' to ask the question.
- Take a quick choral or partner response.
- Mime eating grapes one at a time as you re-read the line.

TEACHER NOTES:
First country: Spain. Foundation students may not understand 'twelve months' yet. If so, briefly explain by counting on fingers.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who think any food can be eaten. Bring them back to grapes.
12:
SAY:
- "Greek families often hang onions on their doors to show growth and new beginnings."
- "At midnight, a lucky guest steps in with their right foot first."
- "A pomegranate is smashed on the ground."
- "The more seeds that scatter, the more luck for the year ahead."
- "Ask: what do Greek families hang on their doors? Expected: onions."

DO:
- Read the page aloud.
- Pause after 'their doors' to ask the question.
- Take a quick choral response.
- Mime smashing a pomegranate with one foot.

TEACHER NOTES:
Greece. The pomegranate detail will come up again on slide 33 with the adjective work. Foundation students will need help with 'pomegranate'. Show the picture or briefly describe a red round fruit with seeds.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who confuse onions and pomegranates. Use the pictures.
13:
SAY:
- "Listen again to the Greek tradition."
- "Greek families often hang onions on their doors to show growth and new beginnings."
- "Ask: what do Greek families hang on their doors? Expected: onions."

DO:
- This slide repeats the Greek traditions content. Use it as a reread or skip if students answered confidently last slide.
- If using, ask one extra question, like 'why do they hang onions?'

TEACHER NOTES:
This slide duplicates content from slide 12. Treat it as a reread or skip if students were confident first time. The repetition may be a slide error - confirm content matches what is shown when teaching.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who notice the repeat. Acknowledge briefly and move on.
14:
SAY:
- "On the beaches of Brazil, crowds dressed in white throw flowers into the sea."
- "They throw small boats of gifts for Lemanjá, the goddess of the ocean."
- "If the waves carry the boats away, wishes come true. Then fireworks brighten the sky."
- "Ask: why do you think wearing white is important? Expected: a tradition, special clothing, peaceful, special."

DO:
- Read the page aloud.
- Pause after 'for Lemanjá' to ask the question.
- Take 1 to 2 responses.
- Affirm any sensible answer.

TEACHER NOTES:
Brazil. The colour 'white' will come up again on slide 34 with adjective work. Foundation students may not know 'goddess'. Briefly explain as 'a special being people believe in'.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who fixate on the fireworks. Bring them back to the white clothes and Lemanjá.
15:
SAY:
- "Eating soba noodles is a favourite New Year's Eve meal in Japan."
- "The noodles break easily, so they remind people to let go of old troubles and make a fresh start."
- "At temples, bells ring 108 times to welcome the year with peace."
- "Ask: what might breaking soba noodles teach people about a fresh start? Expected: let go of old things, start new."

DO:
- Read the page aloud.
- Pause after 'fresh start' to ask the question.
- Take 1 to 2 responses.
- Mime breaking a noodle.

TEACHER NOTES:
Japan. The noodles detail will come up again on slide 35 with the adjective work. Foundation students may not understand the symbolism. Keep it concrete: noodles break easily, so it reminds people to leave old worries behind.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who fixate on eating. Bring them back to the symbolism.
16:
SAY:
- "In New York City, millions watch a giant glowing ball drop in Times Square."
- "As it reaches the bottom at midnight, cheers and music fill the streets."
- "People celebrate together."
- "Ask: what happens in Times Square at midnight? Expected: a giant ball drops."

DO:
- Read the page aloud.
- Pause after 'Times Square' to ask the question.
- Take a quick choral response.
- Mime a ball dropping with your hands.

TEACHER NOTES:
New York. Foundation students may have heard of this. Use the action of a ball dropping to anchor the memory.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who say it is a real ball game. Show that this is a giant decoration.
17:
SAY:
- "German celebrations often include marzipan pigs called Glücksschwein."
- "That means lucky pig."
- "Sharing these sweets is thought to bring good fortune."
- "Ask: what is Glücksschwein? Expected: a marzipan pig, a lucky pig sweet."

DO:
- Read the page aloud.
- Take a quick response.
- Briefly explain that marzipan is a sweet made from almonds.

TEACHER NOTES:
Germany. Foundation students may need 'marzipan' explained. The lucky pig idea is a fun anchor.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who think the pig is real. Reassure that it is a sweet.
18:
SAY:
- "In Denmark, people smash old plates and cups on the doors of friends and family."
- "The more broken pieces you find outside your home, the more luck and love you are thought to have."
- "From grapes to fireworks, noodles to lucky pigs, each country has its own joyful way of welcoming the new year."
- "Ask: how might these traditions help people feel connected to their culture? Expected: doing something special together, family time, something only your culture does."

DO:
- Read the page aloud.
- Pause after 'new year' to ask the question.
- Take 2 to 3 responses about being connected.
- Connect back to Fang Fang's Chinese New Year.

TEACHER NOTES:
Denmark and the closing line. Foundation students will need 'connected to their culture' explained simply: doing the same things as your family or country. Refer back to Fang Fang's Chinese New Year.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who only fixate on smashing things. Briefly explain it is allowed in this tradition, then redirect to the bigger idea.
19:
TEACHER NOTES:
Section divider for vocabulary. The focus word is 'scatter'. Move on to the routine slide.
20:
SOURCES:
Collins Primary School Dictionary, https://schools.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/primary, accessed 16.1.26

SAY:
- "Our word today is scatter."
- "Say it with me. Scatter."
- "When you scatter something, you throw or drop it so it spreads over a large area."
- "In the text, the pomegranate seeds scatter when the fruit is smashed."
- "When planting seeds, you scatter them. People scatter confetti to celebrate."

DO:
- Point to the word.
- Have students choral say it three times.
- Mime scattering seeds with both hands.

TEACHER NOTES:
Follow the four-part vocabulary routine. Movement-based meaning works well for this word. The 'think and move' slide will give students a chance to act it out.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who think 'scatter' means hide. Show the spreading action.
21:
SAY:
- "What does it mean when things scatter?"
- "It is when things move away from each other and do not stay in one group."
- "Ask: tell your partner one example. Expected: birds flying away, leaves blowing, marbles spilling."

DO:
- Read the slide aloud.
- Take a quick partner share.
- Take 2 to 3 responses.
- Affirm sensible examples.

TEACHER NOTES:
This slide unpacks meaning through examples. Foundation students often think of action movies. Steer them to natural examples.

WATCH FOR:
- Students confused. Mime spreading your fingers wide and saying 'scatter'.
22:
SAY:
- "Stand close together with your group."
- "Now... scatter!"
- "Move to different parts of the room."
- "Ask: did you stay in one group? Expected: no."
- "Ask: did you all move in the same direction? Expected: no."
- "Ask: what happened to the group? Expected: it broke up, spread out."

DO:
- Cue students to stand close.
- Say 'scatter!'
- Watch students spread.
- Bring them back together for the questions.

TEACHER NOTES:
Movement activity is the strongest hook for this word. Set clear boundaries (e.g., stay in the room) before saying 'scatter'.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who run too fast or near walls. Stop and remind of safety boundaries.
23:
SAY:
- "Look at the picture."
- "Complete this sentence: The birds scattered because..."
- "Ask: a possible answer? Expected: the dog ran towards them, a loud noise, someone shouted."

DO:
- Read the sentence starter.
- Take a partner share.
- Take 2 to 3 responses.
- Read the modelled answer (the dog ran towards them).

TEACHER NOTES:
This slide builds oral language and uses 'scattered' in context. Affirm any reasonable cause.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who freeze. Prompt 'what would scare birds?'
24:
SAY:
- "Look at the picture of the toys."
- "Ask: which toys are scattered around the room? Expected: the toys spread out everywhere, not in a pile."
- "Show me by pointing."

DO:
- Point to the picture.
- Take 1 to 2 responses.
- Use the spreading action with hands.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Cold Call after Pair Share
Script:
- Ask: which toys are scattered? Expected: the ones spread out everywhere.
- Scan for: students pointing to the right area or naming the right toys.
PROCEED:
- Most students point or name correctly. Move on.
PIVOT:
- Most likely: students name the toys in a pile.
- Reteach: show that 'scattered' means spread out, not piled together.
- Re-check: ask 'is one toy in the corner scattered?' Expected: yes.

TEACHER NOTES:
Visual check.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who point to a tidy stack. Redirect.
25:
SAY:
- "Which fits best with scatter?"
- "Ask: group together or spread out? Expected: spread out."
- "Show me on your fingers, one for group together, two for spread out."

DO:
- Cover the answer.
- Reveal.
- Have students choral say 'scatter means spread out'.

TEACHER NOTES:
Quick synonym check before sentence-level work.

WATCH FOR:
- Students with mixed fingers. Take one of each and ask 'why?'
26:
TEACHER NOTES:
Section divider for sentence-level writing. The focus is orally expanding sentences with adjectives. This builds on Lessons 3 and 4.
27:
SAY:
- "Remember, an adjective is a word that tells us more about a noun - a person, place or thing."
- "Adjectives can tell us about size, colour, shape, age, or quality."
- "Say it with me. Adjective."

DO:
- Read the slide aloud.
- Use the paint brush action.
- Have students choral repeat the meaning.

TEACHER NOTES:
Quick I Do revision. Most students will remember.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who can repeat 'adjective' but not the meaning. Use the paint brush action.
28:
SAY:
- "Read the sentence with me. They eat grapes."
- "Ask: what are the nouns? Expected: they, grapes."
- "We can make this sentence more detailed by adding an adjective."

DO:
- Choral read the sentence.
- Point to each noun.
- Promise students they will get to add an adjective next.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: brainstorm adjectives for grapes together. Set up the next slide.

WATCH FOR:
- Students wanting to suggest adjectives now. Tell them their turn is next.
29:
SAY:
- "What adjectives could we use to describe the grapes?"
- "Ask: what colour are they? Expected: red, green, purple."
- "Ask: what do they look or feel like? Expected: juicy, big, small."
- "Tell your partner one adjective for grapes."

DO:
- Read the slide prompts.
- Take a partner share.
- Take a few responses.
- Affirm sensible adjectives.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: brainstorm adjectives. Use the prompts on the slide if students freeze.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who only say a colour. Push for one more sense.
30:
SAY:
- "Now we add the adjective."
- "They eat blank grapes."
- "They eat juicy grapes."
- "The adjective comes BEFORE the noun."
- "Choral read with me: They eat juicy grapes."

DO:
- Read the slide aloud.
- Highlight the position of the adjective (before grapes).
- Have students choral repeat the new sentence.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: model expanding the sentence. Foundation students need to hear the adjective in the right position.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who place the adjective after the noun. Reset and re-read.
31:
SAY:
- "Look at two sentences."
- "They throw flowers beautiful into the sea."
- "They throw beautiful flowers into the sea."
- "Ask: which has the adjective in the right spot? Expected: the second one."
- "Show me on your fingers, one or two."

DO:
- Cover the answer.
- Reveal.
- Choral read the correct sentence.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Me Fingers
Script:
- Ask: which sentence has the adjective in the right spot? Expected: 2.
- Scan for: most fingers showing 2.
PROCEED:
- >=80% show 2. Move on.
PIVOT:
- Most likely: students struggle to hear the difference.
- Reteach: read both sentences slowly, pointing to where 'beautiful' sits each time.
- Re-check: ask 'does the adjective come before or after the noun?' Expected: before.

TEACHER NOTES:
Threshold check on adjective position.

WATCH FOR:
- Students with mixed fingers. Take one of each and ask 'why?'
32:
SAY:
- "How do we choose the best adjective?"
- "We can ask ourselves these questions."
- "What colour is it? What does it look like? How does it feel?"
- "What shape or size is it? What might it feel like if you touched it?"

DO:
- Read each prompt aloud.
- Choral repeat one prompt.
- Tell students these are tools they can use anytime.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: explain choosing adjectives by considering features (size, shape, colour, visual aspect, texture, feeling). Foundation students need these prompts to generate words.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who do not use the prompts. Praise students who use them on the next slide.
33:
SAY:
- "Listen to the sentence. They smash pomegranates onto the ground."
- "What adjectives describe the pomegranate?"
- "Ask: what colour is it? Expected: red."
- "Ask: what does it taste like? Expected: sweet, tasty."
- "Let's expand: They smash red pomegranates onto the ground."

DO:
- Read the original sentence.
- Use the prompts from the previous slide.
- Take responses.
- Read the expanded sentence with one chosen adjective.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: prompting questions. Connect back to the Greek tradition from the read aloud.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who suggest random adjectives. Use the prompts to focus them.
34:
SAY:
- "In Brazil the crowds dress in blank clothes."
- "What adjectives describe the clothes?"
- "Expected: white, fancy, special, expensive."
- "Let's expand: In Brazil the crowds dress in white clothes."

DO:
- Read the original sentence.
- Take adjective ideas.
- Read the expanded sentence with 'white'.

TEACHER NOTES:
Connect back to the Brazilian tradition. The adjective 'white' is the one from the text.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who say a different colour. Affirm but redirect to what was in the text.
35:
SAY:
- "They break blank noodles in Japan."
- "What adjectives describe the noodles?"
- "Expected: thin, slippery, long, tasty."
- "Let's expand: They break tasty noodles in Japan."

DO:
- Read the original sentence.
- Take adjective ideas.
- Read the expanded sentence.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: prompting questions about noodles. Connect to the Japanese tradition.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who say 'old' (because the noodles break). Affirm but redirect to 'tasty' or 'long'.
36:
SAY:
- "Which adjective would best complete this sentence?"
- "They smash blank cups in Denmark."
- "Ask: rough, strong, or old? Expected: old."
- "Show me on your fingers."

DO:
- Cover the answer.
- Reveal.
- Have students choral read the full sentence.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Me Fingers
Script:
- Ask: which adjective fits, rough, strong, or old? Expected: old.
- Scan for: most fingers showing 3.
PROCEED:
- >=80% show 3. Move to the You Do.
PIVOT:
- Most likely: students choose 'rough' because they think of broken things.
- Reteach: remind them the cups are smashed because they are old, not because they are rough.
- Re-check: ask 'why do they smash old cups, not new ones?' Expected: because old cups are not needed anymore.

TEACHER NOTES:
Threshold check before the You Do activity.

WATCH FOR:
- Students with mixed fingers. Take one of each and ask 'why?'
37:
SAY:
- "With your partner, look at the picture and listen to the sentence."
- "Add an adjective to describe one of the nouns."
- "For example, 'The fireworks exploded' becomes 'The colourful fireworks exploded'."
- "Ready?"

DO:
- Direct students to listen and look.
- Use the next slides to model and try.
- Take a few partner responses.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: Provide adjective picture cards as prompts (slide 43).
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: Add an adjective to BOTH nouns in the sentence (e.g., 'The colourful fireworks exploded loudly' or expand a second noun).

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: display images and say a sentence. Students expand. Some sentences will have more than one noun.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who repeat the same adjective every round. Push for variety using the prompts from slide 32.
38:
SAY:
- "Look at the picture. They drove to the restaurant."
- "Add an adjective to describe the restaurant."
- "Tell your partner."

DO:
- Take partner responses.
- Affirm sensible adjectives like busy, noisy, loud.
- Choral read the new sentence.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: restaurant - busy, noisy, loud.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who describe the action (driving) instead of the noun. Redirect.
39:
SAY:
- "Look at the picture. They looked at the eels in the tank."
- "Add an adjective to describe the eels."
- "Tell your partner."

DO:
- Take partner responses.
- Affirm sensible adjectives like slimy, long, wriggly.
- Choral read the new sentence.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: eels - slimy, long, wriggly. Connect to the eels in Fang Fang's Chinese New Year.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who freeze. Prompt 'what do eels look like?'
40:
SAY:
- "Look at the picture. They ate rice and vegetables."
- "Add an adjective to describe the rice OR the vegetables."
- "Tell your partner."

DO:
- Take partner responses.
- Affirm rice (white, steaming, sticky, delicious) and vegetables (colourful, steamed, cooked).
- Choral read the new sentence.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: rice and vegetables adjectives. This sentence has two nouns. Students may add an adjective to either or both.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick the same adjective for both. Push for variety.
41:
SAY:
- "Look at the picture. Lisa used the chopsticks to eat the dumplings."
- "Add an adjective to describe the chopsticks OR the dumplings."
- "Tell your partner."

DO:
- Take partner responses.
- Affirm chopsticks (long, thin, delicate) and dumplings (steamed, hot, tasty).
- Choral read the new sentence.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: chopsticks and dumplings adjectives. Connect to Lisa trying chopsticks in the read aloud.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who add an adjective in the wrong position. Reread to check.
42:
SAY:
- "Look at the picture. They listened to the fireworks and watched the lion."
- "Add an adjective to describe the fireworks OR the lion."
- "Tell your partner."

DO:
- Take partner responses.
- Affirm fireworks (colourful, bright, loud) and lion (red, bright, colourful, long).
- Choral read the new sentence.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: fireworks and lion adjectives. Final practice in this set.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who can confidently add adjectives to either noun. They are ready for Lesson 8.
43:
SAY:
- "If you need help thinking of an adjective, look at these picture cards."
- "Ask: what is each picture doing or feeling?"

DO:
- Display the cards as needed.
- Use them only with students who freeze.

TEACHER NOTES:
Existing note: optional scaffold. Use only as needed.

WATCH FOR:
- Students leaning on the cards every round. Push them to try without first.
44:
TEACHER NOTES:
Closing credits slide. No teaching needed. Tomorrow students present their recount.
